films.title: ?????? Cinema
films.description:
Totally FREE. No RSVP. First come, first admitted! Doors open 30 minutes before showtime.

Welcome to Seattle's premiere "blindfolded" screening series! The film title will not be announced until the seats are filled and the movieshow is about to commence.

Take the gamble of a chance encounter and discover the movie you didn't know you needed. We aim to provide an enjoyably disorienting experience in which you can indulge your curiosities without any intimidating barriers to entry. And besides, we just think it's sneaky and fun to keep sexy secrets. Don't you?

Movies from all o'er the globe, spanning from the dawn of cinema to its far-flung future. The only criterion is that the Beacon is going to bring out that private stock stuff every single time. We're giving you films that haven't been played to death, proffering an alternative history of cinema, a celebration of the breadth and depth of film history, a pulsating motion picture party.

films.title: 2026 Collide-O-Scope Halloween Show
films.description:
Collide-O-Scope’s Halloween celebration, a beloved Seattle tradition, returns from the beyondwith a one-of-a-kind found-footage phantasmagoria of hilariously hair-raising film freak-outsand outrageous oddball video! A deliriously demented cavalcade of expertly crafted montage,packed with absurd pop culture ephemera, obscure oddities, and awesome music — all remixedand mashed up into an evening of eerily epic entertainment. It’ll leave you gasping with laughterand clutching your little melted face! Plus, frightening fabulous prize drawings!

For over 16 years, Collide-O-Scope has been slaying Seattle audiences with their singular brandof entertainment, and their legendary Halloween extravaganza is not to be missed!

Costumes are encouraged, but there is no costume contest.

films.title: 5Point Film Fest 2026
films.description:
Adventure is coming to North Bend on November 8! Pro Ski and Mountain Service is hosting 5Point Film Festival - On The Road, an evening of inspiring short films from the acclaimed 5Point Film Festival, founded in Carbondale, Colorado.

This film program features some of the year’s most unforgettable stories of adventure, perseverance and the human spirit—all curated with the heart and soul that 5Point is known for. Whether you're a lifelong outdoor enthusiast or simply love a good story, these films are sure to move, challenge and ignite your sense of adventure.

From wild expeditions to urban athletes to environmental advocacy to intimate character-driven stories, 5Point OTR captures the joy, risk, and revelation of a life lived outside the comfort zone. Each short film is handpicked to reflect 5Point’s guiding principles: Respect, Commitment, Humility, Purpose and Balance.

films.title: A Man and a Woman
films.description: This New Wave-style bitter-sweet romance took the world by storm, playing for a year and a half straight in Seattle. Persistence of emotional pain vies with the prospect of future happiness for an adult woman and man. Anne (Anouk Aimee, stunning and mysterious) works in the film industry and mourns her dead husband (Pierre: Pierre Barouh), killed in an accident. Jean-Louis (Jean-Louis Trintignant), a race car driver, lost his wife (Valérie Lagrange) to suicide. Chance brings Anne and Jean-Louis into proximity: her daughter and his son attend the same boarding school North in Deauville. There’s a spark between them, but what can come of it; they’re both in love with those who’ve departed. Writer-Director Lelouch engages us in Anne’s and Jean-Louis’ separate lives, thrillingly as he drives in the Le Mans and the Monte Carlo Rally races (Trintignant’s uncle won many races; for car aficionados: the film features Ford GT40s, early Mustangs). For Anne, her lost Pierre remains a felt presence, but she and Jean-Louis drive together in all weathers. They met by chance, and chance generates more suspense: are they really made for each other? Anouk Aimee is one of the screen’s enigmatic beauties, and Lelouch knows to enshrine her face: “It is women’s faces that speak.” What does she say?

films.title: A Nightmare on Elm Street
films.description:
1, 2, Feeddy's coming for you...

Nancy Thompson and her friends all share the same disturbing image in their dreams: a horribly disfigured man with knives on one hand. They soon learn this man is not just a figment of their imagination, and if they flal asleep, there's a very good chance they may never wake up.

Robert Englund plays the iconic Freddy Krueger in Wes Craven's horror classic. Heather Langenkamp stars as Nancy, one of cinema's most quintessential final girls. The film also features Johnny Depp's big screen debut as her boyfriend Glen.

films.title: A Simple Machine
films.description:
A Simple Machine is the award-winning, debut feature from director Mark Alan Hoffman, featuring a breakout lead performance by rising star Richard Blackmon. A true indie from the PNW, it is a quietly profound tour-de-force stunningly shot by cinematographer Kevin Fletcher (It’s What’s Inside) and scored by renowned composer Mark Orton (The Holdovers, Nebraska).

As the country looks to mark its 250th anniversary amid deep uncertainty, this story offers rare respite - a modern-day, cinematic Walden - a luminous, deeply human meditation on personal freedom, economic independence, and the cost of wanting less in a culture built on more.

“…relevant to almost everyone in America, as affordability becomes one of our biggest worries.” —Tim Molloy, MovieMaker

films.title: A Year of School
films.description: Set in 2007, the film follows Fred, an 18-year-old Swedish girl who moves to Trieste to complete her final year of high school and take her graduation exams. Upon arriving, she discovers she is the only girl in a class full of boys, immediately becoming the center of attention. Eager to make friends and find her place, Fred disrupts the established dynamics of a close-knit trio: Antero, Pasini, and Mitis, who all try to impress her. As she compromises to fit in, Fred realizes she is constantly being tested for acceptance. How much of ourselves are we willing to sacrifice to belong?

films.title: Actually, It Is Rocket Science
films.description:
Actually, It Is Rocket Science is the newest chapter in TGR’s ongoing study of the fall line, told through the world’s best skiers as they turn the mountain into a laboratory and every descent into an experiment.

The study spans Bute Inlet, British Columbia; Haines, Alaska; Japan; Finland; Andorra; Montana; Jay Peak, Vermont; and Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Different mountains, snowpacks, conditions, and approaches—but the same forces are always at work: speed, gravity, instinct, and consequence.

Actually, It Is Rocket Science is a tongue-in-cheek look at the seemingly reckless abandon that many of the world's best snow athletes display as they push the physics of what is possible. Athletes explore the intricacies of dissecting a big mountain line, the physics and amplitude of a massive gap, calculating transition, and the force of gravity.

So, is it rocket science—or is it not?

Watch closely and decide for yourself.

Locations: Jackson Hole, Wyoming, Haines Alaska, British Columbia, Japan, Finland, Andorra, Jay Peak, Vermont, Montana

Athletes: Kelly Hilleke, Teal Harle, Colter Hinchliffe, Kai Jones, Maggie Voisin, Nick McNutt, Parkin Costain, Karl Fostvedt, Keegan Killbride, Tim Durtschi, Thibault Magnin, Anna Tedesco, Tucker Carr, Wyatt Gentry, Lalo Rambaud, Jasper Skidmore, Daniel Johnson, Jerermy Emmer, Rylan Messner, Andrew Bird, Dylan "Dro" Roide, Nicholas Johnson, Luke Price, Seamus O'niell, Andreya Zvonar, Jackson Lalla , Adrian Hayden, Bode Tracy

Part of the MOUNTAIN FILM FESTIVAL 2026!

films.title: Again Again
films.description:
What happens after Groundhog Day ends? What happens when the protagonist has to contend with life post-time loop, in all of its messy permanence? Again Again, the debut feature from Aberdeen-raised filmmaker Mia Moore, puts a singularly queer spin on that very question. Moore herself stars as Aggie, a foul-mouthed, pot-smoking trans woman who awakens from a ten-year time loop into a new day. But a decade, it seems, wasn't nearly enough time for Aggie to sort out her on-again-off-again relationship with her childhood best friend, Tess (Aria Taylor).

Executive produced by pioneering filmmaker Lilly Wachowski, Again Again is heady yet intimate, asking existential questions while staying tightly focused on a trans woman's subjectivity. Over the course of a single day, which Aggie promises Tess will be "one normal day with none of that time garbage," the two friends bum around Aberdeen, revisiting their shared past and negotiating their uncertain future. Again Again is steeped in gloomy Aberdeen atmosphere, from the gritty shipyards to the demolition derby. Yet Aggie remains haunted by what she witnessed in "the loop." When she starts to unravel the mystery of what—and who—caused the time loop in the first place, Aggie must choose the future once and for all.

—Alison Jean Smith

“Again Again tasks its characters to live their lives as if today were their last and the unknown possibilities of tomorrow were far from a given. And it wants everyone in the audience to do the same. It’s scary stuff. It’s also beautiful.” – Sara Michelle Fetters, Seattle Gay News

films.title: All I Desire
films.description:
Barbara Stanwyck has spent ten years convincing her family that she's become a famous actress. Unfortunately, her career hasn't quite lived up to the publicity. In Douglas Sirk's ALL I DESIRE, she returns to her small Wisconsin hometown for her daughter's school play, where her arrival causes considerable excitement among people who have spent the last decade discussing her disgrace. Her youngest daughter worships her, her eldest daughter resents her, and her estranged husband (Richard Carlson) has grown accustomed to a life without her. To complicate matters, an old lover (Lyle Bettger) is still hanging around town, apparently under the impression that ten years is a perfectly reasonable amount of time to wait for a woman who wants nothing to do with you.

Adapted from Carol Ryrie Brink's novel Stopover, ALL I DESIRE is one of Sirk's most intimate and affecting films, a beautifully observed melodrama about the lives we imagine for ourselves and the people we disappoint along the way. Stanwyck is extraordinary as a woman who has spent so long pretending to be someone else that returning home requires an entirely different kind of performance. Sirk finds enormous feeling in the smallest gestures, particularly the gulf between a daughter who idolizes the mother she barely knows and one who remembers exactly what it was like to be abandoned by her. At just 79 minutes, it's a wonderfully rich little movie, with Stanwyck finding vanity, humor, and unexpected tenderness in a woman who has spent ten years rehearsing her triumphant return and now has to face the people who know better.

films.title: American Werewolf in London
films.description: After a terrifying encounter with a mysterious wolf in the English countryside, two American tourists are forever changed. One man dies from his injuries, while the other begins a horrifying transformation into a werewolf. He must confront the terrifying reality of his condition and the looming threat of the next full moon, all while being hunted by professionals determined to stop the savage beast he's becoming.

films.title: Artists and Models
films.description:
In the 1950s, America became convinced that comic books were corrupting the minds of its young people, filling their heads with violence, perversion, and dangerous fantasies. Director Frank Tashlin took one look at this national emergency and decided to make a movie about how great all that sounded. Jerry Lewis plays a comic book addict whose feverish dreams of the voluptuous Bat Lady keep his roommate Dean Martin awake at night—until those same nocturnal ravings become the inspiration for a bestselling comic strip. Add Shirley MacLaine and Dorothy Malone as a pair of suspiciously gorgeous upstairs neighbors, a few Communist spies, and a government investigation, and you've got a movie that makes a pretty convincing case for the pleasures of having your brain permanently destroyed by pop culture.

A former cartoonist himself, Tashlin transforms Cold War paranoia, sexual repression, and the American publishing industry into a delirious explosion of Technicolor lunacy, with enough outrageous sight gags, shameless innuendo, and exposed thighs to warrant an investigation by the Senate. Admired by Jean-Luc Godard and celebrated as a precursor of Pop Art, Tashlin makes the whole world look like a Looney Tunes cartoon that has recently gone through puberty. But beneath all the hysteria, ARTISTS AND MODELS is also one of the great movies about goofing off with your roommate, making art with your friends, and finding happiness in a country that would very much prefer you stop doing all three.

films.title: Auntie Mame
films.description:
"Life is a banquet--and some poor suckers are starving to death." Mame Dennis

When young, impressionable Patrick Dennis' millionaire father dies, the boy is left in the care of his only living relative--his flamboyant, extravagant, devil-may-care ... and never, never dull Auntie Mame. New York during the Jazz Age--Despite the best efforts of estate executive Dwight Babcock (Fred Clark) to rear Patrick (Jan Handzlik and Roger Smith) as a boring, stuffy aristocrat, the boy is swept into Mame Dennis' (Rosalind Russell) world of parties, flappers and the most eccentric, entertaining, intelligent set of friends anywhere. Through the stock market crash, a marriage to a rich Southerner and his death while scaling the Alps, Mame's whirlwind approach to life opens Patrick's eyes to endless possibilities. Based on the hit Broadway play and the novel by Patrick Dennis. Golden Globe Award winner for Actress in a Leading Role - Musical or Comedy (Rosalind Russell), Picture - Comedy Six Academy Award nominations: Best Picture Best Actress in a Leading Role (Rosalind Russell) Best Actress in a Supporting Role (Peggy Cass) Best Cinematography, Color Best Art Direction-Set Decoration, Black-and-White or Color Best Film Editing

films.title: Beavis and Butt-Head Do America
films.description:
Shaken awake by a typically anxiety-addled Beavis with the terrible news that their beloved television set has been stolen, fellow slacker Butt-Head slowly pieces together a horrifying new reality: this sucks. No longer able to coast on the waves of MTV, the dimwitted delinquents exit their squalid dwellings in a desperate search that quickly entangles them in a plot to “do” a seedy criminal’s wife for a sizable sum. Hoping to finally score, the couch potatoes embark on a national quest from Las Vegas to Washington, DC. From underground animation to Hollywood extravaganza to further revivals, Mike Judge’s giggling mouth breathers remain an unshakable presence in the cultural milieu of America with their evergreen image of slackerdom and distinctly ‘90s charm. All roads lead to the Great Cornholio.

35mm print courtesy of Paramount.

films.title: Beloved
films.description: Presented by Cinema Italian Style. Two women face opposing fertility struggles: a young Nunzia grapples with an unplanned pregnancy while longing for carefree days, as Maddalena, at 40, desperately tries to conceive a child.

films.title: Beware! The Devil's Wrath - Special Screening
films.description: Blackwood Falls is a Texas town where faith, family, and community reign supreme - until recently married outsiders Richard and Samantha unwittingly disrupt the fragile tranquility. The beautiful Samantha draws the watchful gaze of restless high school boys, leading to a fateful encounter that plunges the couple into tragedy. A shocking act of violence creates unimaginable loss and leads to a wave of mysterious, ritualistic attacks that threatens to reveal the small-town’s secrets. The killings evoke hooded specters, flaming visions, and unholy judgments that force residents to question their own complicity. Paranoia spreads like wildfire: are these acts divine retribution, demonic forces, or something more human? Their descent into confusion and terror uncovers layers of hypocrisy beneath the community’s pious exterior, building to a confrontation that tests the limits of vengeance and redemption.

films.title: Blood Rage
films.description:
"Thanksgiving isn’t Thanksgiving without a viewing of BLOOD RAGE." - Joseph A. Ziemba, BLEEDING SKULL!

Todd and Terry are twin bros with twin problems -- namely, one of them is an axe-wielding maniac! After a literal drive-in massacre, Todd is blamed for the carnage and institutionalized, while Terry goes free. Ten years later, Todd escapes from an asylum on Thanksgiving aka it’s time for blood to raaaaage!!

Produced by whip-smart filmmaker Maryanne Kantor, directed by John Grissmer (SCALPEL), and shot in Florida, BLOOD RAGE is what happens when you combine Thanksgiving, 1970s TV star Louise Lasser, a killer synth score, and the most unbelievable gore effects in all of slasherdom, courtesy Ed French (TERMINATOR 2). Just remember, “It’s not cranberry sauce!”

films.title: Breathless
films.description:
“Cinema repeats itself; first as tragedy, then as farce.” - theriverjordan

Widely dismissed upon release for daring to remake Jean-Luc Godard's sacred New Wave classic, Jim McBride's BREATHLESS takes the original's fascination with American popular culture and pushes it into a state of complete delirium. Where Godard found romance in the cool detachment of Parisian gangsters, McBride plunges headfirst into the overheated fantasies of rock and roll, comic books, American machismo, and the terrible decisions people make in the name of love.

Richard Gere plays Jesse Lujack, a car thief, cop killer, Jerry Lee Lewis fanatic, and quite possibly the most obnoxiously romantic man in Los Angeles. His idea of true love involves convincing a beautiful French student (Valérie Kaprisky) to abandon her entire life and run away with him to Mexico. Gere throws himself into the role with such reckless enthusiasm that it's sometimes difficult to tell whether Jesse is the coolest man alive or the biggest idiot in the world. Beneath all the swagger is a genuinely strange portrait of a man who has absorbed so much American popular culture that he can no longer distinguish between romantic devotion and performing the part of a romantic hero.

“It’s not just one of the great remakes but one of the great, largely unsung, American films of the 80s.” - Justin LaLiberty

films.title: Brunello: The Gracious Visionary
films.description: In the documentary film Brunello: the Gracious Visionary, Giuseppe Tornatore imagines a symbolic card game between Brunello and a mysterious opponent—an allegory of Cucinelli’s life. As the unseen rival plays his hand, the film traces Brunello’s journey in a lyrical narrative, blending cinematic reconstructions, archival footage and intimate testimonies. Each chapter of his life is marked by affectionate nicknames: “little fox” from his grandfather, “young lord” from his father, “the German” from colleagues, and “the wolf” from his wife. A poetic, almost medieval canticle, the film bears Tornatore’s unique signature, elevated by Nicola Piovani’s score.

films.title: Buffalo '66
films.description:
Few movies look or feel quite like Vincent Gallo's BUFFALO ’66, a beautifully deranged romantic fantasy in which the dreary landscape of upstate New York becomes the setting for one man's elaborate exercise in self-pity. Shot on gorgeously faded 35mm, the film is full of extraordinary visual inventions: flashbacks that invade the present, musical numbers that materialize out of nowhere, and Christina Ricci performing an exquisite tap dance to King Crimson in a deserted bowling alley. It's a movie of almost embarrassing personal obsession, with a visual imagination capable of making even its ugliest impulses look irresistible.

Gallo plays Billy Brown, a recently released convict who kidnaps a young woman (Ricci) and forces her to impersonate his wife during a visit to his spectacularly unpleasant parents (Anjelica Huston and Ben Gazzara). Billy is controlling, verbally abusive, and almost impossibly self-absorbed, while Ricci's Layla responds to his increasingly appalling behavior with a devotion that seems to defy all reasonable explanation. Their relationship has all the makings of a hostage situation because, of course, that's exactly what it is. Yet Gallo films this grotesque arrangement with the tenderness of a great love story, inviting us to fall in love with a fantasy that ought to make us deeply uncomfortable. The result is a film whose beauty and cruelty are so thoroughly entangled that it's difficult to separate what makes it moving from what makes it disturbing.

films.title: Cameraperson
films.description: A boxing match in Brooklyn; life in postwar Bosnia and Herzegovina; the daily routine of a Nigerian midwife; an intimate family moment at home: these scenes and others are woven into Cameraperson, a tapestry of footage captured over the twenty-five-year career of documentary cinematographer Kirsten Johnson. Through a series of episodic juxtapositions, Johnson explores the relationships between image makers and their subjects, the tension between the objectivity and intervention of the camera, and the complex interaction of unfiltered reality and crafted narrative. A work that combines documentary, autobiography, and ethical inquiry, Cameraperson is both a moving glimpse into one filmmaker’s personal journey and a thoughtful examination of what it means to train a camera on the world.

films.title: Candy Mountain
films.description:
A rock ‘n’ roll odyssey from New York into the wilderness of Nova Scotia, Candy Mountain follows down-on-his-luck Julius, a generally unpleasant dude and mediocre musician to boot (Kevin J. O’Connor), who develops a get rich quick scheme: track down the reclusive guitar maker Elmore Silk. The journey up the road, full of wrong turns and dead ends, finds Julius confronting and frequently upsetting the disgruntled personalities that the ever elusive Silk left in his wake, from scorned family members (Tom Waits as Silk’s nouveau riche brother, a wheelchair-bound Dr. John as his cranky son in law) to abandoned lovers (Bull Ogier). Reportedly a challenging co-directorial collaboration, the film nonetheless registers as a delectable synthesis of Robert Franks photographic eye (as found in his canonical "The Americans") and the road mythologizing seen throughout the work of cult novelist Rudolph Wurlitzer (Two-Lane Blacktop, Walker, Pat Garrett And Billy The Kid). Spread out in the back seat for what Jonathan Rosenbaum calls a “wry, laid-back ‘Heart of Darkness.’”

35mm print courtesy of Museum of Fine Arts Houston.

films.title: Cartoon Happy Hour
films.description: It's the Happiest Hour for the whole family! Two hours of classic cartoons to get your weekend started off right. We have kid friendly snacks and drinks. We also have adult friendly snacks and drinks! Every Thursday 5:00 until 7:00.

films.title: Castration Movie Chapter iii. Junior Ghosts—Premorphic Drift; a fragmentary passage
films.description: Castration Movie is a multi-part postmodern epic by visionary auteur Louise Weard. In Chapter iii. Junior Ghosts—Premorphic Drift, Izzy (Avalon Fast) seeks out everything in her power to stop her partner (Henri Gillespi) from transitioning.

films.title: CatVideoFest 2026
films.description: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CatVideoFest 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations and shelters alike — a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need.

films.title: Clash by Night
films.description:
After ten years of disappointment, Barbara Stanwyck's Mae Doyle returns to her California fishing hometown looking for something resembling a decent life. In Fritz Lang's CLASH BY NIGHT, she marries a good-hearted fisherman (Paul Douglas) who offers her the security she's never had, only to find herself dangerously attracted to his best friend (Robert Ryan), a married movie projectionist who appears to hate his wife, his job, and just about everyone he's ever met. Stanwyck knows perfectly well what kind of man he is, which only seems to make matters worse. Marilyn Monroe nearly steals the picture as a tough, outspoken cannery worker with a much less accommodating attitude toward the men in her life.

Adapted from a play by left-wing dramatist Clifford Odets, CLASH BY NIGHT is a bitter, bruising examination of marriage, sexual desire, and the limited choices available to women in working-class America. Lang opens with extraordinary documentary footage of Monterey's fishing industry, establishing a world of hard physical labor before turning his attention to the equally exhausting business of living with other people. What follows is a remarkably unsentimental melodrama in which everyone wants something they can't quite name, nobody seems capable of leaving well enough alone, and even the most ordinary conversations threaten to become acts of mutual destruction. Stanwyck and Ryan are magnificent together, their attraction fueled as much by contempt as desire. Few films are quite so attentive to the ways people turn their most intimate relationships into instruments of self-punishment, or so understanding of why they keep doing it.

films.title: Clayface
films.description: Matt Hagen's meteoric rise from Gotham street kid to Hollywood leading man is tragically cut short when a local crime boss's actions leave him horribly disfigured. Abandoned by his team and with nothing left, Matt seeks out a cutting edge treatment that miraculously returns him to his former self… but also unexpectedly affects his grip on reality, spiraling him down a destructive path of all-consuming revenge.

films.title: Delicatessen
films.description:
A delicious French love story. The perfect film for a late night date!

A butcher hires a handyman to take care of the apartment building he owns, as all the previous ones have disappeared not-so-mysteriously. But the butcher's meaty plot hits a snag when his daughter and the new handyman develop tender feelings for each other.

Part of Central Cinema's Food'n'Family month!

In French with English subtitles.

films.title: Dracula of Exarcheia
films.description:
A mad orthopedist arrives in Athens from the Carpathians, settles in the anarchist neighborhood of Exarcheia, and starts robbing graves for the body parts of dead musicians. His plan: stitch together the perfect rock band and make a fortune. Unfortunately, the dead have other ideas. Soon Athens’ militant zombies are organizing against the exploitation of their remains.

Part Hammer horror spoof, part punk-rock musical, part political satire and part document of the Greek underground at the dawn of the ’80s, Nikos Zervos’ gloriously disreputable cult oddity throws Frankenstein, Dracula, John Waters, socialist zombies, sexual anarchy and the real-life rock band Mousikes Taxiarhies into a blender. Tzimis Panousis leads a who’s-who of Greek counterculture through 87 minutes of passionate politics and absolute nonsense, culminating in a concert for the living and the dead.

A one-of-a-kind blast of Greek surrealism that has to be seen to be believed.

films.title: Elisa
films.description: Elisa, thirty-five, has been in prison for ten years, convicted of killing her older sister without apparent motive and burning her body. She claims to remember little to nothing of the crime, as if she had drawn a veil of silence between herself and the past. But when she decides to meet with criminologist Alaoui and take part in his research, in a tense and relentless dialogue memories begin to take shape, and in the pain of fully accepting her guilt, Elisa glimpses, perhaps, the first step toward a possible redemption.

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Beyond Borders
films.description:
This seemingly disparate collection of films takes us beyond the often artificial boundaries of countries, equipment, formats, frames, genres, species, states, and styles.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Some Place to Stand (Sandy McLennan | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 4:04 | CA)

An Expo ’67 song on 45, current hand-processed film footage, reflecting on social concepts then and now.

The Spider (Shanna Maurizi color/sound | 16mm to digital | 8:45 (time updated?) | US)

Nighttime visions emerge from a dusty roadside and out of the depths of the subconscious as two characters are drawn together by a shared experience. “The Spider” mines family history by developing an ancestral mythology where time is simultaneous, but loss is real.

Hurricane Season (Michelle Trujillo | b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 6:22 | US)

Hurricane anxiety takes a visceral form as the image searches for an escape route. Inspired by true events. Created on 16mm film and developed with comfrey, mint, yerba mate and willow leaves.

Jonah (Daniel Cortés Ramírez | b&w/sound lomokino to digital *wide* | 10:40 | Colombia)

Jonah, the anti-prophet, escapes once again from the god who humiliated him.

He boards a ship to Tarshish, and out on the vast sea, a distant yet familiar echo calls to him. His body trembles from the trauma, but a deep embrace gathers him up and holds him close.

This film uses 35mm Lomokino footage to imagine an alternative fate for the perpetrators’ violence.

En La Paz (Jeremy Moss | b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 3:00 | US/Bolivia)

Created in-camera on a rooftop in La Paz, Bolivia in July on B&W reversal film with my Bolex as dusk was approaching. The city’s sea of antennas and surrounding mountains pointing to the sky inform the film’s sound.

Kaze No E (or Why the Wind Whispers Among the Leaves) (Takahiro Suzuki | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 7:05 | US)

Four young researchers in Big Sky Country begin to wonder about the vastness of the world and greater cosmos. If non-human presences were capable of harboring intelligence and communicating, what information could they pass along? Using the trees and wind as messengers, the researchers record and decipher writings and recordings from the trees and wind, relating them back to the land and universe, before finding ways to embody them through sound and movement as a form of empathy and communion with a greater intelligence.

Transmission (Douglas Urbank | b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 7:20 | US)

Layers of patterns generate sound.

Toss a Rose Over (Janelle VanderKelen | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 10:44 | US)

The green ones share stories of change in this travelogue from the vantage point of plants. In a canyon where all things move, these ancient beings urge humanity to reconsider acts of interspecies and intraspecies relation during a current period of anthropogenic climate change.

Leaf Peeper (Vito Rowlands | color/sound | Super 8 to digital | 2:54 | US)

A frantic frolic in Fall foliage. A stop-motion autumn adventure. A symphony in blaze orange.

Run (Robert Schaller | b&w/silent | 11:51 | 16mm print | US)

An optical quest to capture the feeling of running through the Colorado mountains on and around the Continental Divide.

Alpine Tundra (Kathleen Rugh | color/sound | 5:35 | 16mm print | US)

At an elevation of 14,264 feet above sea level, the peak of Mount Blue Sky is too harsh for trees and common vegetation. Instead, the ground is covered with fragile tundra grass, weak soil, and rock. In this harsh climate exists the highest paved road in North America, that allows visitors traveling by car to partake in striking views and a sense of awe in the extremes of nature.

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Expanded Cinema Performance and Film
films.description:
FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

No Landscape Ever Made Me Cry (Sujin Lee | b&w/silent | 5:30 |16mm to digital | US/Korea)

I am a crier, and this film tells stories about holding back (or not holding back) tears; words break down and often turn into crying. The film tries to explain those tears. It also reflects an ambivalent attitude—being personal while trying to maintain distance from these emotions, wanting to talk about crying but not quite being able to. Produced on 16mm film using inkjet-printed paper and plastic negatives, the entire process was cameraless.

Pedra e Montanha, Expanded Cinema Performance of 35mm Slides by Tetsuya Maruyama (3-35mm slide projectors + live sound accompaniment by Corey J. Brewer | 50:00 | Brazil)

A continuation of ongoing research into contemporary mining activities in Brazil and beyond. Multiple 35mm slide projectors cycle through images captured by a Brazilian mining company while being manipulated live by the artist using three 35mm slide projectors. Live sound accompaniment by local artist/musician Corey J. Brewer incorporates field recordings taken by Maruyama and Brewer (check for accuracy).

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Pattern and Place
films.description:
Inspired by Eric Stewart’s description of his film as “a quiet study in pattern and place,” these films closely observe phenomena, not limited to but often privileging the natural world. 2 films will be shown on 16mm and the last is an expanded cinema performance.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Maya at 24 (Lynne Sachs | b&w/sound | 4:47 | 16mm to digital | US)

Lynne Sachs films her daughter Maya in 16mm black and white film, at ages 6, 16 and 24. At each iteration, Maya runs around her mother, in a circle – clockwise – as if propelling herself in the same direction as time, forward. Conscious of the strange simultaneous temporal landscape that only film can convey, we watch Maya in motion at each distinct age.

Solar Wave (Christina Nguyen | color/sound | 2:53 | 16mm to digital | US)

sun light, sun set, sun rise, sun ray. a hand processed in camera roll shot on Kodak 3383 color print stock.

Hemispheres (Eric Stewart | color/sound | 7:14 | 16mm to digital | US)

Filmed over the course of several years in southern Colorado, Hemispheres is a quiet study in pattern and place, as observed through the window of my living room. Shot on Super 16mm film, the project layers multiple time-lapse exposures of cacti and seasonal light, capturing subtle shifts in color, atmosphere, and rhythm. Like the inlay of a sundial meeting a garden’s creeping vines, what emerges is not a photograph of a singular view or moment, but a composite drawing of duration—using light to trace the intersecting cycles of growth and dormancy, brightness and shadow, warm and cool, seasonal progression and retreat…

Stock (Lucy Ellis | color/sound | 1:50 | 35mm to digital | UK)

Stock uses both new and obsolete digital stock imagery transferred onto 35mm film through UV printing, pen plotting and sticker transfer. Drawing parallels between the vertical storage of information digitally and on the film surface, the imagery transfers from one storage system to another allowing for a shift in line, texture and detail, a drift from digital precision. Undertaking a new form of light and a new identity (from digital to analog) the imagery becomes slow in its formation whilst unstable in nature.

Licht & Ton (Light & Sound) (Jan Rehwinkel | b&w/sound | 5:50 | Germany)

A film without a camera: The fascination of painting tone or noise—a composition of visible sound and audible images. After experimenting with photograms on 16mm film, whose technical precision proved too much for me, I decided to switch to what I like best about filmmaking: painting what I want to see (and hear!) onto the material myself. When I work this way, I am constantly confronted with failure or the impossibility of perfection – even the contact printer I used to make the screening copy was unpredictable. But I see all of this as a creative tool and integrate it into the process.

Fluss (Penny McCann | b&w/sound | 3:39 | 16mm to digital | CA)

In this experimental film, a journey down the Danube River is transformed into a dream space of half-seen images and flickering shorelines. Though at times abstract, the river remains certain, always moving towards the sea. Filmed in black and white 16mm and hand-processed, Fluss is a companion to River (2023), a black and white study of the Ottawa River in winter. Commissioned by Ottawa’s Lightproof Film Collective.

Drift (Tessa Garland | b&w&color/sound | 7:25 | S 8 to digital | UK)

Shot on Super 8, the film captures a walk around a precarious, low-lying sandbank island, where fleeting observations come into focus only to vanish again. Rotations and cycles ebb and flow through manmade wind vanes assembled from foraged sea drift, while sea-worn objects hint at deeper meanings beneath the surface. Prehistoric-looking cacti punctuate the island, contributing to its strange, otherworldly atmosphere.

Phytophonics (Karel Doing | color/sound | 4:18 | 16mm to digital | UK)

Plant matter is used to create finely detailed indexical traces on photochemical film. The traces are not only visible but also audible. By feeding botanical textures, patterns and rhythms into the optical sound system noise, cracks, pops and hiss is generated. Seeing is hearing. Such a cross modality disobeys the usual lipsync illusion and replaces this so called realism with a radically different concreteness. Phytophonics is serious play with living material in a world that is increasingly based on simulated sham. Eco-punk against the abyss created by late-capitalism.

Spring Song (Wei Gao | color/sound | 16:21 | 16mm to digital | Korea/France)

“Spring Song” was filmed from 2016 to 2024. Every spring, the filmmaker, armed with a Super 8mm camera and using the vibrant colors of Ektachrome super 8 film, or Kodak color negative film, captured the vibrant blossoms, grasses, leaves, insects, and small animals of spring. The filmmaker’s meticulous daily observations in her own rooftop garden, as well as her chance encounters in the National Forest Park, revealed a rich natural ecosystem. She also employed cameraless photography, creating images of plants through photochemical reactions between Super 8mm film, plants, and organic matter. She then combined these Super 8mm and cameraless images together to create a dynamic and colorful vision of spring. In the context of increasingly strained ecological environments, the director created a living green ecosystem in her rooftop garden, observing plants and practicing a lifestyle integrated with nature.

Gradually Forming a Circle (Zack Parrinella | color/sound | 8:02 | 16mm print | US)

A stepped and steady progression of a line becoming a circle. Soundtrack by Zekarias Musele Thompson.

The Rocks: Kata Tjuta West of Ularu (Dianna Barrie and Richard Tuohy | color/sound | 6:00 16mm print | AU)

Looking at the present, as though the far future were dreaming of its ancient past – an ‘iconogenic’ vision of Australia.

Mounds Above the Earth (Jaiyi Chen | color/sound | 7:39 | *35mm, 16mm and interventionist tools, performed by Spencer Sundell | US)

“Mounds Above the Earth” contemplates ecological cycles, perception, and environmental transformation, anchored in the rare emergence of two periodical cicada broods surfacing simultaneously for the first time in more than two centuries. The film follows the flicker of red through the cicadas’ developing eyes, a blood moon, and a retelling of an ancient fable.

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Rankin Renwick Solo Show
films.description:
Engauge is thrilled to welcome back Portland, OR-based artist Rankin Renwick, this time to present their work in a solo show. All films by Rankin Renwick.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Toxic Shock (color/sound | 2:50 | S8 to 16mm | 16mm print | 1983)

A visceral personal response to surviving a near-fatal case of Toxic Shock Syndrome. Toxic Shock combines intimate taboos of needles, blood and tampons with tried and true hands-on self-defense, set to a spare, penetrating and unknown score provided by a cassette tape gifted by a forgotten friend. A call to arms; what will you do in defense of your body?

Portrait #1: Cascadia Terminal (color/sound | 6:00 | 16mm hand processed and tinted to digital | 2005)

A 6-minute mesmerizing stare at the most historically efficient grain terminal at the port of Vancouver, B.C. The Canadian Pacific Railway services the terminal, which can unload up to 300 cars in 24 hours, a pace equal to approximately 25,800 tons of prairie grain. Why are we so attracted to the power of industrial sites? Many kids used to hang out here, get high and make out; it has the feel of a ruin though it is still in operation. A huge compound on the water within the city of Vancouver, Cascadia Terminal expands the spirit and gives the feeling of space, of being maybe further out in the country. There even used to be a squat for a bit, in an industrial building near the property. The gentle intimacy of the beautiful score invites us to step into the landscape, but sadly due to Homeland Security measures affecting coastal ports enacted since this filming, we are no longer allowed.

Note: The Portrait Series is part of an ongoing series of filmed places, stories and histories of Cascadia with scores by musicians living in the Pacific Northwest. Portrait #3: House of Sound (2009) will screen later in this program. Portrait #2: Trojan screened at EEFF 2025.

Britton, South Dakota (b&w/sound | 9:00 | 16mm to digital | 2003)

Ivan Besse managed the Strand movie theater in Britton, South Dakota during the Depression. Besse owned a 16mm camera and used it to shoot people at their various activities around town during the day. He screened the local footage before feature films and newsreels as a lure to entice paying customers into the theater. Of the 2 1/2 hours of footage, most of it depicts townspeople walking down the street; there are also scenes of a barn being moved, a cornhusking contest and kids running out of a school. What really stands out is 8 minutes of children’s portraits. The subjects–dressed in what appears to be their Sunday best–clearly had no notion of a movie camera. The lack of an overt narrative creates a sort of cinematic paper doll environment–the film invites viewers to drape these images with futures, which have long since become histories. The drone of Johnne Eschleman’s accompanying melancholy organ composition casts a tragic shadow over these bright faces, one that may or may not have come to pass.

Crowdog (b&w & color/sound | 7:00 | Super 8 to digital | 1984/1998)

An early encounter with Peter Mathiessen’s 1983 book In the Spirit of Crazy Horse concerning the fallout of the FBI’s ‘Reign of Terror’ over the American Indian Movement led a teenaged filmmaker on a pilgrimage to the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota. This journal entry of a film describes a young artist in the midst of over two years of shoe-free peregrinations, with a spare, mesmerizing narration that reflects a landscape ranging from the slimy underbelly of dirty Chicago to a hitchhiker’s perch in the back of a dusty pickup truck. See the kindness of the older self who dares also to show us the convictions of our youth. Bare feet on a paved road, a white girl stands to one side of a white line, a wolf dog weaves and dances before the camera.

Yawn (color/sound | 2:00 | 16mm to digital | 1998)

Two sublime minutes of the human experience: the color orange, piano, a wordless documentary on both the inhale and the exhale. The unspoken challenge: can the viewer last without joining the fray?

Olympia (b&w/sound | 11:00 | S8 to digital | 1984/1998)

The ultimate origin story, eleven grueling minutes of a home birth. Midwives and friends surround a naked woman bulging with life as she endures the last eternal moments of her pregnancy and a child arrives. The grainy, black-and-white super-8 film softens the visual experience, while the pulsating soundtrack recalls approaching helicopters or jackhammer job-sites–birth from the point of view of the forthcoming baby. The camera never flinches; even as the new human crouches on m30 ama’s flattened belly and the music eases into hypnotic low string meditations, and the viewer aches for release into the comfort of the family circle, still the afterbirth must emerge before the film pulls back to reveal an ordinary living room, an ordinary day.

9 is a secret (b&w/sound | 6:00 | 16mm and video to digital)

“Renwick recounts a sad time in her life, when a friend was dying and she suddenly became aware of the presence of crows. The dark birds in turn point her to the practice of counting crows, which is both a children’s rhyming game and a form of divination in which the number of crows suggests events in the future. Eight crows augur death: nine crows reference a secret. Renwick combines these fragments with glimpses of imagery – a bed, the crows captured as silhouettes, a man’s twisted body – to craft a lyrical and moving essay that works its magic through poetic accretion rather than narrative logic.” –Holly Willis, L.A. Weekly

Crackhouse (color/sound | 2:30 | S8 to digital | 2015)

Mosaic artist Jeffrey Bale, described by the New York Times as a ‘rock star’, transformed a former Portland crack house into a stone art paradise, an urban sanctuary and bird haven. Crack House, edited in camera, is a cosmic burst of color and sound created to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the introduction of Super 8 film.

Portrait #3: House of Sound (b&w/sound | 11:22 | 35mm to digital | 2009)

In the 1950s, Williams Avenue had the most significant concentration of Blacks living in Portland. In the late ‘50s, pushing an ‘urban renewal’ policy and exercising the power of eminent domain, the Portland City Council condemned almost the entire neighborhood to replace it with the Memorial Coliseum, Rose Quarter and Emmanuel Hospital. Edited film and an edited 5-hour radio show dedicated to the memory of the House of Sound record store, this is a eulogy for the former community center and for all the places up and down the street that used to fill those empty lots, now unrecognizable as mixed-use, high-rise hyper-urban development.

SF Hitch (b&w & color/sound | 5:17 | S8 and 16mm to digital | 2012)

Shot and edited over the span of three decades, SF HITCH recounts the artist’s experience of hitch-hiking with their feisty canine companion from Chicago to San Francisco in 1981. Both visuals and narrative are woven together with the agility and vitality of Beat poetics—a reflection of the experience of unmoored travel and an homage to the very artists they meet upon arrival.

“My wolf dog Zeb and I set off hitching in the early 80’s from Chicago to SF to see what it’s all about. We met some beats and some freaks.” – Rankin Renwick

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Tactility and Memory
films.description:
These films posit a connection between the haptic world and what we choose to embody, remember, erase, perhaps forget. Filmmakers manipulate the medium in a variety of ways to emphasize visual texture and showcase techniques that evoke memory and touch.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Caribou (Lindsay Aksarniq McIntyre | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 15:00 | CA)

An experimental documentary created with handmade and manufactured emulsions exploring the close and enduring connections between Inuit, caribou, lichens, and land use. Lichen developers help bring the images to life, while caribou hide is processed into gelatin to make handmade emulsion. Filmed primarily on the land in Nunavut where caribou struggle to maintain their lifeways amidst burn events, habitat disruption and changing conditions.

I Found Some Old Footage of a Tree (Krista Lee Steinke | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 3:22 | US)

An experimental film that unfolds as a glimpse into the creative process: a sketch, a vignette, a visual mind map, and a meditation on how to document a planet in flux. In this piece, the materiality of film becomes a metaphor for time, impermanence, and the fragility of the natural world. Working with Super 8mm and 16mm footage, the image itself carries traces of transformation, decay, and memory, blurring the boundaries between document and artifact. A sense of anxiety and urgency shapes the work, leaving us uncertain whether we are witnessing the past, the present, or a message from the future. Ultimately, the film asks how cinema can hold onto a world that is continually changing, and what remains when both landscapes and images begin to disappear.

EOJ (Tianming (Alaric) Zhou b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 2:22 | China/US)

Regulatory signs shot on 16mm, hand-processed with caffenol, and subjected to both analog and digital corrosion. EOJ reimagines the anxiety induced by caffeine hypersensitivity and the pressures of social conditioning.

Autopsia del Río (Ada Rajkovíc | color/sound | Super 8 to digital | 2:37 | US)

Inspired by David Gatten’s “What The Water Said,” this film uses the material of Super 8 celluloid itself to record the memories of the Río de la Plata, a former burial ground for los desaparecidos during Argentina’s military dictatorship.

Flow Attachment (Tijana Petrovic | b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 8:40 | US)

A coastal sand dune is transformed and reshaped into digital ether. The film focuses closely on sand as a material, which is composed of silica, the mineral that is a primary ingredient in manufacturing silicon chips, lenses, binoculars, microscopes and mirrors – devices that extend our vision. The film uses these devices to visually capture the sand dune and evoke the transformation of materials that goes into their production. Through 16mm analog techniques, elemental forces of a sand dune merge with the physical properties of the celluloid.

Polychora (Abinadi Meza | color/sound | 16mm to digital | 9:22 | US/Mex)

A cameraless 16mm film, scanned to 4K and slowed into extreme temporal dilation: an aqueous prism where chromatic membranes evolve. Its title evokes the polychoron, a four dimensional form. Fractal traces surface within the color fields: analog and digital, cellular and cosmic, coexisting in the same luminous space. Polychora functions as a neuro refuge, a haptic cinema where the eyes and body can rest inside something vast.

Tactile Light Diary (Callon Murphy | b&w/sound | 8mm to digital | 6:00 | CA)

Touch replicated through audiovisual means./Fabric structures exposed and magnified.

Textiles dance over microphone and screen./Images burst to the forefront.

First a beach, then an unclean pool./Summer slips into fall./ Details are forgotten or misremembered./The retained memory of tactile objects.

Need and Desire (Francesca Svampa | color/sound | Super 8 to digital | 8:24 | Spain/Italy)

A gesture of erasure. A spell. If you lift the emulsion from a photograph, destroy its surface, transplant it onto a new body, does the memory it carried survive? “Need and Desire” originates from this question, and from the poetic belief that making a film can alter reality. The cinematic act becomes [an] incantation: a process that destroys and reconstructs simultaneously. Still memories become an “emulsional” landscape.

Fata Morgana (Hannu Nieminen | color + b&w/sound | Super 8 to digital | 5:16 | Finland)

Fata Morgana is a mirage phenomenon in which distant objects appear distorted, often floating or stretched out on the horizon. The film is an experimental study of memory, images and filming, and how memories can transform, rust and disintegrate. The photographs are from a summer spent on the banks of the Terijoki River in Karelia, which [the] Soviet Union took from Finland after WWII.

Interwoven Intervals (Laura Kraning | b&w/sound | 16mm to digital | 6:00 | US)

Pattern drafts are the graphical score for weaving – grids of light and dark representing the over and under of weft threads between the warps. In this material hybrid of film and textile, the graphic repetition of grids, lines, and squares assert a structural form that is fragile and vulnerable to erasure.

La Duréte du Mental/Mental Toughness (Charles-Andre Coderre | color/sound | 35mm to digital *wide* | 20:00 | CA)

“It’s a distraction for many, a profession for a few, when for me sport is my whole life. And if fighting is the reason you’re living. If every muscle clamors : train me, exercise, put on a sprint. Find a competitor or at least fight against a pole. It’s hard to get started but it’s otherwise difficult to stop. Even with your back against the mat. Never mind. You have to stand up and go further. You will now have to fight against yourself.” Transforming Olympic wrestling and pole vaulting Soviet films from the 1980s into expressive, painterly imagery, the film appears as a film practitioner’s decathlon.

films.title: Engauge 2026 – Tainted
films.description:
This program gathers a group of films that confront the various underbellies of life: deceptive icons, devastated landscapes, climate change, predatory advertising, drug addiction, toxic politics and environmental disasters, among others, using found footage emulsion lifting, documentary techniques, handmade film and cameras, single framing, and narrative strategies.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Front Ear Theory (Brady Lewis | color/sound | 5:12 | S8 to digital | US)

“Front Ear Theory” is a five-minute history lesson. To be more precise, it’s a story about a history lesson. Or about a history teacher. It’s an experimental narrative that was shot entirely on super-8 (mostly Kodachrome) film.

Bigger Than Us, The Berkeley Pit, Butte, Montana (color/sound | 9:00 | 16mm to digital | US)

A portrait of a huge open-air copper mine in Butte, Montana. The closed mine dominates the city geographically, and also financially, culturally, historically, and in the on-going health effects from the highly toxic metals and chemicals which fill the bright blue-green water in the pit. (The pit is a designated Superfund site.) After a few opening titles which briefly introduce us to the pit and its history, the film becomes a wordless visual montage, almost always superimposing several layers of footage.–David Finkelstein.

Blu/Blue (Andrea Nevi | color/sound | 4:47 | Super 8 to digital | Italy)

A community displaced by a climate disaster settles in a new habitat, where memories of their former way of life slowly begin to resurface. BLU is an experimental climate fiction short film made entirely from Super 8mm found footage recovered from a flea market.

Injured? (Eislow Johnson | color/sound | 13:28 | 16mm to digital | US)

Need help? Crashouts, manifestation influencers and injury lawyers collide in this breakneck ride through the Midwest. 50 years after attorney ads were first legalized in the U.S., their ubiquitous self-portraits (allegedly) invoke a churn-and-burn economy of volume, velocity, fears and veneers.

What You Don't See (Karl Nussbaum | color/sound | 1:25 | 16mm to digital | US)

This film is about what the audience doesn’t see when we watch a film – the sprockets, the optical soundtrack, the splicing tape, the celluloid itself, the frame lines, etc. This is a very short Direct Animation film I made at MONO NO AWARE in Brooklyn. It’s totally analog and was made using only 16 mm and Super 8 found footage film strips.

On The Glue (Dave Johnson | color/sound | 3:02 | 16mm to digital | CA)

From the depths of London, England’s Barracks district amongst the derelict weapons huts, comes a public service expose from the 1970s revealing “THE HORRORS” of kids participating in the act of glue sniffing. The narrative is told in three parts: The reporter, a mother, and her “addict son” David. This film and its title have been appropriated from a 1970’s BBC expose. The visual treatment exposed the footage (and the filmmaker) by gluing pieces of film together then ripping it apart. This becomes an interesting metaphor of creating using the substance of the problem presented in the film. The film was edited by hand and sequenced using measurements to time each shot.

The Gloaming (Charlotte Pryce | color/sound | 14:00 | 16mm to digital | US)

A metaphorical tale of pyrophytic transmutation, of metamorphosis through fire. Inspired by medieval paintings of celestial portents, The Gloaming is a work of bio-mysticism that takes the form of a fable. The slippage between substances and the ethereal nature of matter finds a parallel in the chemical accretions of the hand processed film. In a time of environmental uncertainty, the film offers a story of adaptation and survival.

Thought/Action (Dirk De Bruyn | color/sound | 10:27 | 16mm to digital | AU)

Initiated in 1996 and belatedly completed in 2026, this home-processed 16mm film material was inspired by Marc Adrian’s Total (1968) and incorporates Moucle Blackout and Laszlo Dudas’s voices. Partially shot at Hearst’s San Simeon Castle, Canada and Royal Melbourne Show, it is an exploration of overcoming traumatic thoughts through materialist actions onto the film surface. The completion gap demonstrates the power of and resistance to traumatic events.

Better Lighting (Kathryn Ramey | color/sound | 2:13 | 16mm to digital | US)

An agitprop made from two 30-second GE adverts from the 1970s repurposed to rebuke the role white women voters in the US have chosen to uphold white supremacy and the patriarchy instead of supporting the interests of women and anyone who loves them.

Necropolis (Kevin T. Allen | color/sound | 8:53 | Super 8 to digital | US)

A Stone Tape film inspired by the yellow fever epidemic in 19th century New Orleans, using analog camera techniques and contact microphones to excavate the material traces of trauma. Coined by archaeologist and parapsychologist T.C. Lethbridge, Stone Tape Theory posits that material objects record traumatic events of the past…and that they can be played back.

Good Neighbors Care (Kate E. Hinshaw | color/sound | 3:50 | 16mm to digital | US)

For decades chemical company DuPont and its subsidiary Chemours poisoned North Carolina’s drinking water through illegally dumping forever chemicals into the Cape Fear River. On altered 16mm film, corporate promises of community care and pure water dissolve as rivers and bodies merge in a meditation on what it means to exist in an imperfect environment.

North (Hogan Seidel | b&w/sound | 3:00 | 16mm to digital | US)

I found a decaying print of Nanook of the North and continued its collapse through photochemical processes, confronting the violence of its legacy. “North” is not a restoration, but a reckoning—an act of holding damaged images until they blur, bleed, and refuse the gaze that once claimed them.

Assets (Christine Lucy Latimer | color/sound | 2:22 | 16mm print | CA)

Hundreds of digitally generated filters and assets used by online content creators to simulate a “shot on film” aesthetic are collaged together on expired 16mm Ektachrome. Random contemporary approximations of film artifacts, ranging from industrial to experimental, move through the frame in impossible trajectories. A film of transitions that never transition, positioning moving image signifiers in a post-truth era.

Ashes to Ashes (Sidney Gordon | color/sound | 5:00 | 16mm print | CA)

“Ashes to Ashes” depicts fragments of the artist’s diary as they undergo physical and emotional transformation through a blazing agricultural landscape. Words turn to ash as the past is consumed by flames. Rivers ignite from embers, flow through vessels and begin to crack. Manifested through the land and material processes lies a situated reflection on recovery, loss and evolution. The film was shot at the 2024 Independent Imaging Retreat. It was developed with common comfrey and contaminated wood ash foraged from the farm and was coated in the artist’s blood.

films.title: Engauge 2026 – We Are All Together
films.description:
This phrase, borrowed from Lynne Sachs’ film “A Month of Single Frames,” perfectly captures the relationality that this program embodies: birth, death, motherhood, illness, widowhood, friendship, family, gender, artistry. These films, deeply anchored in the challenging realities of the everyday, are ultimately uplifting.

FILMS IN THIS PROGRAM:

Explant/Implant (Josh Weisbach | color/sound | 3:16 | 16mm print | US)

A lifetime of surgeries continues with an upgrade in battery life and a downgrade in scar tissue when the filmmaker has his original pacemaker replaced after sixteen years.

Objectionable Fruit (Gabby Follett and Hogan Seidel | color/sound | 15:00 16mm to digital | US)

“Objectionable Fruit” is an experimental documentary examining the Ginkgo tree—a living fossil celebrated for its resilience and unique capacity to change sexes, defying human-imposed binaries. Using the Ginkgo as a metaphor for fluidity and endurance, the film weaves together themes of gender identity, ecological interconnectedness, and the nuanced complexities of trans existence.

Dyade (Carole Thibaud & Bertille LaFarge | b&w/sound | 6:50 | 16mm to digital | France)

A film made by two sisters, filmmaker and dancer. Written by four hands, shot and danced in turn. Witness to a shared experience, created through the inspiration of the moment, the light, and the place. A story of gesture, transmission, play, and poetry. The film images were shot in 16mm at the Bressieux farm (Savoie, France) in February 2023, developed in Mire’s shared laboratory in Nantes, and edited back and forth.

You May Laugh at Me a Little (Yuula Benivolski | color/sound | 22:35 | 16mm to digital | CA/Palestine)

A film about a glassblower in Hebron—a place historically known for glass production, which dominated the region for centuries. Each family in the business was known for their own traditional recipe. A couple of years ago I interviewed the last glassblower in Hebron’s old city, and filmed him during a regular day at his studio.

The Algae (Ursula Brookbank | b&w/sound | 5:45 | 16mm to digital | US)

Three sisters of sorrow bring tears and comfort to a widow.

Moving Feelings (Rendro Aryo | color/sound | 5:38 |Super 8 to digital l Indonesia)

An experimental poetry film shot using a super 8 mm camera from 1975. A film that plays with poetry through poetic images. A man and a woman searching and questioning the meaning of youth.

To My Son (Linda Fenstermaker | color/sound | 6:40 | 16mm to digital | US)

A visual exploration on the transition to motherhood and how time shifts in this phase of life seen through the landscapes of the Pacific Northwest.

A Month of Single Frames (Lynne Sachs | color/sound | S 8 to digital | US)

In 1998, filmmaker Barbara Hammer had a one-month artist residency in the C Scape Duneshack which is run by the Provincetown Community Compact in Cape Cod, Massachusetts. The shack had no running water or electricity. While there, she shot 16mm film with her Beaulieu camera, recorded sounds with her cassette recorder and kept a journal. In 2018, Barbara began her own process of dying by revisiting her personal archive. She gave all of her Duneshack images, sounds and writing to filmmaker Lynne Sachs and invited her to make a film with the material.

“While editing the film, the words on the screen came to me in a dream. I was really trying to figure out a way to talk to the experience of solitude that Barbara had had, how to be there with her somehow through the time that we would all share together watching her and the film. My text is a confrontation with a somatic cinema that brings us all together in multiple spaces at once.”

— Lynne Sachs

films.title: Escape From New York
films.description: In 1997, a major war between the United States and the Soviet Union is concluding, and the entire island of Manhattan has been converted into a giant maximum security prison. When Air Force One is hijacked and crashes into the island, the president (Donald Pleasence) is taken hostage by a group of inmates. Snake Plissken (Kurt Russell), a former Special Forces soldier turned criminal, is recruited to retrieve the president in exchange for his own freedom.

films.title: Fatherland
films.description:
Fatherland centres on the relationship between the Nobel Prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Hnrns Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) - actress, writer and rally driver. In the summer of 1949, at the height of the Cold War, father and daughter embark on a challenging and emotional road trip in a black Buick taking them across a Germany in ruins - from US dominated Frankfurt to Soviet controlled Weimar. Returning home after sixteen years of exile in the US, Thomas Mann has to face not only a divided fatherland, but also a deep fracture within his own family.

With Fatherland, Pawlikowski picks up where he left off with his award-winning Ida and Cold War, exploring – in his elliptic, distilled style - the themes of identity, family, love and guilt amid the turmoil and confusion of post-war Europe.

films.title: Five Minutes to Die!
films.description:
It's FIVE MINUTES TO LIVE... HALLOWEEN EDITION!

Here's the deal. You buy a ticket. We show you the first five minutes of five different mystery movies. Then everybody votes on which one to watch in its entirety!

You've got FIVE MINUTES TO DIE! Come have an encounter with the unexpected free from the burden of preconceptions. Choose your own adventure in the unimaginably vast world of strange and interesting cinema. Experience the delight of pure surprise. We'll promise a wild time if you promise to be open to anything.
